record.paper_title: Twenty Open Questions in Supersymmetric Particle Physics
record.original_question: Many supersymmetric and string-motivated theories contain moduli such as Polonyi fields, string-size moduli, the dilaton, MSSM flat directions, or GUT-breaking Higgs fields, whose potentials can be extremely flat and whose couplings to matter can be weak. Do these moduli dominate the early-universe energy density, overclose the universe, dilute baryon asymmetry, or disrupt nucleosynthesis, and what mechanisms—fast decays, thermal inflation, special initial conditions, dilaton stabilization, or parametric resonance—make their cosmology viable?

evidence.quote: The essence of the moduli problem is that fields with extremely flat potentials and weak couplings to other fields tend to be cosmologically dangerous.

These include (but are not limited to): string moduli whose VEV’s ∼ MPl parametrize the size of compact dimensions; the string dilaton whose VEV ∼ MPl parametrizes the string coupling constant; D- and F-flat directions of the MSSM... and Higgs fields responsible for breaking GUT’s to the MSSM.
There are many questions still to be answered about parametric resonance, the conditions under which it will occur, and the means by which the decay products thermalize.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider supersymmetric and string-motivated extensions of the Standard Model that contain scalar "moduli" fields — for example Polonyi-type hidden-sector scalars, string compactification moduli whose vacuum expectation values of order the Planck mass M_Pl parametrize the size of compact dimensions, the string dilaton whose VEV ~M_Pl parametrizes the string coupling, D- and F-flat directions of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, and GUT-breaking Higgs fields. Such moduli typically possess very flat potentials (with masses set by the soft SUSY-breaking scale, m ~ O(TeV) or below) and couplings to ordinary matter suppressed by inverse powers of M_Pl, so they are long-lived and easily displaced from their late-time minima in the early universe.

Within this setting, determine:

(a) Under what conditions a coherent oscillation of such a modulus comes to dominate the energy density of the universe after inflation, and whether its energy density combined with its late decay is compatible with (i) the present critical density bound (no overclosure), (ii) the preservation of any pre-existing baryon asymmetry against entropy dilution from modulus decay, and (iii) the success of Big Bang nucleosynthesis (i.e. decay before t ~ 1 s or with decay products that do not photodissociate light nuclei).

(b) Which of the following mechanisms, or combinations thereof, can render the cosmology of these moduli viable: rapid perturbative decay (requiring sufficiently large modulus mass, m ≳ O(10–100) TeV); a late epoch of "thermal inflation" driven by a flaton field that dilutes the modulus abundance; tuned or dynamically selected initial conditions that place the modulus near its true minimum after inflation; explicit dilaton stabilization mechanisms (e.g. racetrack or Kähler-stabilized potentials); and non-perturbative depletion via parametric resonance / preheating, including precise criteria for when such resonance occurs and how the decay products thermalize.

Provide quantitative bounds linking the modulus mass, initial misalignment amplitude, reheating temperature after inflation, and decay width, that delineate the cosmologically allowed region of parameter space.
artifact.status_search_result: The cosmological moduli problem remains an active research topic. A 2022 JHEP study and a 2015 critical review (arXiv:1502.07746) both indicate the problem persists in general SUSY/string frameworks: while heavy moduli (m ≳ 100 TeV) can decay before BBN, non-thermal gravitino production and LSP overproduction from moduli decay still generically conflict with dark-matter bounds, and no universally accepted resolution exists. Mechanisms such as thermal inflation, large-volume stabilization, and parametric resonance are partial fixes but face their own constraints. Hence the broad question is still open.

status_evidence.title: The cosmological moduli problem and naturalness
status_evidence.snippet: Examines the cosmological moduli problem and its connection to electroweak naturalness; finds non-thermal gravitino production from moduli decay remains problematic.
status_evidence.claim: The moduli problem persists in general SUSY models as of 2022.

status_evidence.title: Cosmological Moduli and the Post-Inflationary Universe: A Critical Review
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews CMP in three parts: BBN constraints, moduli-induced gravitino problem, and LSP overproduction.
status_evidence.claim: CMP is still an open, multi-faceted problem.

status_evidence.title: Higgs, Moduli Problem, Baryogenesis and Large Volume Compactifications
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses moduli problem in large-volume string compactifications and possible resolutions.
status_evidence.claim: Ongoing work attempts but does not fully resolve the moduli problem.
